Multiple lines of animal evidence indicate that moringa contains bioactive chemicals—particularly isothiocyanates and antioxidant/flavonoid compounds—that support peripheral nerve regeneration by improving axonal and Schwann cell responses, reducing oxidative stress, and enhancing functional recovery after sciatic nerve injury; however, human clinical evidence is limited and more translational work is needed to define effective compounds, doses, and delivery for nerve repair in people.<cite id="eac3bd38-2">Crude leaves of Moringa oleifera (200 mg/kg) improved sciatic functional index, grip strength, and sensory thresholds in mice with sciatic nerve lesions while restoring gastrocnemius muscle mass</cite><cite id="eac3bd38-3">Moringa leaf extract stimulated neuronal outgrowth and survival in vitro and exhibited neurotrophic and neuroprotective properties</cite><cite id="eac3bd38-4">Polar moringa metabolites in rodent chow accelerated functional recovery and controlled oxidative stress and glycemia to facilitate nerve regeneration</cite><cite id="85ea44f5-1">The isothiocyanate sulforaphane, a naturally occurring Nrf2/HO-1 activator, accelerated murine sciatic nerve regeneration with increased repair Schwann cell proliferation, improved grip strength and nerve conduction, and enhanced remyelination</cite><cite id="85ea44f5-0">Erucin (another moringa isothiocyanate) promotes proliferation and survival of Schwann cells in vitro and supports axon regeneration</cite> 

What “nerve cell regeneration” entails (context)
- After peripheral nerve injury, axons distal to the lesion degenerate (Wallerian degeneration) while Schwann cells dedifferentiate, clear debris, and create a growth-permissive, aligned scaffold that guides regrowing axons; trophic factors (e.g., NGF, BDNF, CNTF) and extracellular matrix support neurite outgrowth and remyelination, but regeneration is slow and can fail, especially with reperfusion injury and oxidative stress.<cite id="542c0ea0-0">Schwann cells upregulate NGF receptors after axotomy, and reestablishment of axon–Schwann cell contact suppresses receptor expression at the regeneration front</cite><cite id="542c0ea0-2">In vivo labeling traced adult mouse sensory axon regeneration across a crush site, with slow initial growth followed by faster, steady elongation</cite><cite id="542c0ea0-4">Tissue-engineered axon tracts accelerate regeneration via direct axon-facilitated axonal regeneration and enhanced Schwann cell infiltration/alignment</cite> 

Whole-plant moringa evidence in animal models of nerve injury
- Moringa oleifera leaf powder and extracts improved motor and sensory function after sciatic nerve crush in mice, with significant gains in sciatic functional index, grip strength, and pain thresholds; the study also noted gastrocnemius muscle mass restoration and glycemic stabilization, consistent with a regenerative microenvironment conducive to axon reinnervation.<cite id="eac3bd38-2">Moringa leaves (200 mg/kg) improved sciatic functional index, muscle mass, and grip strength, and restored sensory function in mice with sciatic nerve injury</cite><cite id="eac3bd38-3">Moringa leaf extract stimulates neuronal outgrowth and survival and has neurotrophic and neuroprotective properties</cite><cite id="eac3bd38-4">Polar extracts in rodent chow at 2 g/kg/day accelerated sensory and motor recovery and reduced oxidative stress, supporting faster nerve regeneration</cite> 
- Mechanistically, moringa’s rich phytochemistry—glucosinolates, flavonoids (e.g., quercetin/apigenin), phenolic acids, saponins, and more—has been linked to antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective actions that can protect neurons, preserve axonal integrity, and support trophic signaling during injury and repair; however, the injury-repair–focused trials above primarily tested crude or broad-spectrum extracts rather than single compounds.<cite id="542c0ea0-3">Moringa is a rich source of alkaloids, saponins, tannins, steroids, phenolic acids, glucosinolates, flavonoids, and terpenes with antioxidant and neuroprotective potential</cite><cite id="eac3bd38-3">Phenolic acids, glucosinolates, and flavonoids in moringa underlie antioxidant and neuroprotective effects, with neurotrophic and neuroprotective properties shown for leaf extracts</cite> 

Key chemical classes in moringa and how they promote nerve regeneration
- Isothiocyanates (from glucosinolates): Moringa contains sinigrin/erucin-type isothiocyanates that directly support Schwann cells and axon growth. Erucin promotes proliferation and survival of repair-oriented Schwann cells and supports axon regeneration in vitro, consistent with a mechanism that increases the number and function of the glial “growth highways” that guide regenerating axons.<cite id="85ea44f5-0">Erucin promotes proliferation and survival of repair Schwann cells and supports axon regeneration in vitro</cite>

Scope, caveats, and what’s still uncertain
- Evidence base: The strongest mechanistic link to “nerve regeneration” comes from isothiocyanates (erucin/SFN) and antioxidant/flavonoid-rich moringa extracts showing accelerated Schwann cell proliferation, reduced oxidative stress, and improved functional and electrophysiological recovery in rodent models; whole-plant powders and metabolite-enriched diets improved motor/sensory recovery after sciatic crush. - Human/clinical gap: Direct clinical trials of moringa-based regimens for nerve repair in humans are scarce; although moringa is widely used in folk medicine and has antioxidant/neuroprotective properties, rigorous nerve-injury–specific human studies defining dosing, compound selection (e.g., SFN vs erucin vs quercetin), route, and timing are needed. - Mechanistic complements: Engineered or diet-delivered regenerative scaffolds and trophic support can accelerate regeneration by both axon-facilitated propagation and enhanced Schwann cell alignment—mechanistic parallels to moringa’s likely effects suggest combined pharmacologic and biomaterial strategies may potentiate clinical outcomes if and when translated.<cite id="542c0ea0-4">Tissue-engineered axon tracts accelerate regeneration via direct axon-facilitated regeneration and Schwann cell–mediated pathways</cite> 

How to apply this knowledge practically
- For research/clinical exploration: Prioritize isolating and delivering moringa-derived isothiocyanates (erucin, SFN) and phenolic/flavonoid fractions with proven trophic and antioxidant activities, timed to the “regeneration window” after injury; combine with metabolic glycemic control and reperfusion injury mitigation given the demonstrated benefits of oxidative stress control and functional readouts in vivo.<cite id="85ea44f5-1">Sulforaphane timing (immediate post-injury) and Nrf2/HO-1 activation improved regeneration and function</cite><cite id="eac3bd38-4">Polar phenolic-rich metabolites reduced oxidative stress and accelerated nerve regeneration with functional gains</cite> 
- For patients: Moringa leaf powder and moringa-rich diets may support nerve health via antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions, but there are currently no established, guideline-based regimens for nerve repair; patients with nerve injury should continue standard care (surgical repair for transections, splints, physiotherapy), manage diabetes and vascular risk factors, and discuss any complementary therapy with their clinician, especially if on blood-thinning or chemotherapy drugs. Clinical trials are needed to confirm safety and efficacy in nerve repair and to define dosing and delivery.<cite id="eac3bd38-3">Moringa shows neurotrophic and neuroprotective properties, but evidence for nerve regeneration after injury is scarce and more study is recommended</cite> 

What would close the gaps
- Randomized, blinded clinical trials in human patients with surgically confirmed sciatic or peripheral nerve injuries, testing standardized moringa leaf extract or isolated moringa compounds (SFN, erucin, quercetin/apigenin) against placebo or standard care, with outcomes including nerve conduction studies, electromyography, MRI/SWI for myelination, SF-36 quality of life, and return-to-function timelines; mechanistic biomarker panels (HO-1/Nrf2 activation, Schwann cell proliferation markers, GAP-43/BDNF, oxidative stress metabolites) would validate the proposed pathways demonstrated in animals.<cite id="85ea44f5-1">Murine data show mechanistic and functional improvements with sulforaphane that should motivate human translational studies</cite><cite id="eac3bd38-2">Crude moringa leaf powder improves functional recovery in mice and warrants further therapeutic development</cite>

- Moringa contains bioactive chemicals—especially isothiocyanates and antioxidant phenolics/flavonoids—that can promote nerve regeneration by enhancing Schwann cell proliferation and trophic support, reducing oxidative and metabolic stress, and improving functional recovery in rodent models of sciatic nerve injury; however, human clinical evidence is limited and more rigorous trials are needed to establish dosing and efficacy in nerve repair.<cite id="eac3bd38-2">Moringa leaf powder improved functional recovery after sciatic nerve injury in mice</cite><cite id="85ea44f5-1">Sulforaphane activated HO-1/Nrf2, increased repair Schwann cells, and improved nerve conduction and remyelination in mice</cite><cite id="85ea44f5-0">Erucin promoted Schwann cell proliferation/survival and axon regeneration in vitro</cite><cite id="eac3bd38-4">Polar moringa metabolites reduced oxidative stress and accelerated functional and nerve regeneration</cite>

Title: Enhancement of Heme-Oxygenase 1 in the Injured Peripheral Nerve Following Sulforaphane Administration Fosters Regeneration via Proliferation and Maintenance of Repair Schwann Cells
Snippet: Nuclear erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) and its downstream effector heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1) are commonly activated in response to cellular stresses. The elevated expression of HO-1 has been associated with markedly accelerated peripheral nerve regeneration. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of a naturally occurring dietary Nrf2/HO-1 activator—sulforaphane (SFN)—on regeneration in a murine sciatic nerve crush model. The beneficial safety profile of SFN has been thoroughly investigated and confirmed several times. Here, SFN was administered daily, starting immediately after C57BL/6 mice were subjected to sciatic nerve crush injury. Injured sciatic nerves were excised at various time points post injury for molecular, immunohistochemical and morphometric analyses. Moreover, functional assessment was performed by grip strength analysis and electrophysiology. Following SFN treatment, the early response to injury includes a modulation of autophagic pathways and marked upregulation of Nrf2/HO-1 expression. This enhancement of HO-1 expression was maintained throughout the regeneration phase and accompanied by a significant increase in repair Schwann cells. In these cells, elevated proliferation rates were observed. Significant improvements in grip strength test performance, nerve conduction velocity and remyelination were also noted following SFN treatment. Collectively, SFN modulates cytoprotective and autophagic pathways in the injured nerve, increasing the number of repair Schwann cells and contributing to effective nerve regeneration. Given the availability of SFN as a nutritional supplement, this compound might constitute a novel regenerative approach with broad patient accessibility and further studies on this topic are warranted.
</snippet>

Title: Peripheral Nerve Regeneration Following Crush Injury to Rat Peroneal Nerve by Aqueous Extract of Medicinal Mushroom Hericium erinaceus (Bull.: Fr) Pers. (Aphyllophoromycetideae)
Snippet: Peripheral nerves may be subjected to crush injuries in a variety of circumstances, including motor vehicle accidents, fractures, dislocations and natural disasters such as earthquakes [20]. After injuries to peripheral nerves, axons and myelin sheaths distal to the lesion are degraded. The degenerative products are eliminated by the cooperative action of denervated Schwann cells and infiltrating macrophages. Wallerian degeneration serves to create a microenvironment favoring axonal regrowth. Schwann cells within the endoneurial tubes of the distal nerve dedifferentiate towards a non-myelinating proliferative phenotype that over-express growth factors, cell adhesion molecules and extracellular matrix to promote regeneration [1]. 

In contrast to nerve transection injury, nerve crush injury causes less severity, because it leaves the basement membrane of Schwann cells surrounding the original nerve fibers intact and thus, despite the disrupted axon cylinder, enables Schwann cells to provide pathways to guide the regenerating axons [21]. Although crushed peripheral nerves keep anatomical continuity, regenerate spontaneously and somehow reinnervate their target tissues, the longer it takes for the crushed nerve to reinnervate their target tissues, the greater the chance of permanent denervation atrophy of the target tissues. Therefore, accelerated nerve regeneration is crucial to obtain satisfactory functional outcomes [22]. 

Functional deterioration following crush injury is not only related to the impact of the crush itself, but also includes other important components such as ischemia of the limb. Studies on crush injury models in peripheral nerves have shown better functional recovery when therapies were directed against ischemia-reperfusion injury by using antioxidants, lipid peroxidation inhibitors and anti-inflammatory agents [23]. With this in mind, the present study evaluated the nerve regeneration activity of H. erinaceus which possesses antioxidant activity as an alternative herbal pharmacotherapy for peripheral nerve repair [24]. 

The functional recovery as assessed by PFI scores in couple with histological examination of regenerated nerves and target EDL muscle revealed that aqueous extract promoted peripheral nerve regeneration.
</snippet>

Title: Nanosuspension of Foeniculum Vulgare Promotes Accelerated Sensory and Motor Function Recovery after Sciatic Nerve Injury
Snippet: Peripheral nerve injuries generally result in the loss of motor and sensory functioning of nerves, often leading to permanent physical disability. The functional loss arises from the degenerate axons and the damage to the integrity of Schwann cells (SCs). A number of integrated cellular mechanisms coordinate axonal regenerations for functional retrieval after nerve injury [1,2]. A growth-permissive environment is created by the non-neuronal SCs for injured axons. A number of structural and molecular changes appear in distal and proximal stumps of the injured nerves, as a mechanistic approach to support the regeneration of axons [3]. Injured neurons cause the downregulation of mRNAs involved in neurotransmissions and the upregulation of those required for regeneration. As an immediate response, the growth-associated proteins (GAP)-43, tubulin, and actin, are upregulated to provide a conducive environment for nerve regeneration [4]. Thus, the injured nerves possess the inherent potential for regeneration, generally a complicated and slow process [5][6][7]. A progressive decline is observed in upregulated biomachinery that slows down the regeneration of axons, prolonging the process of nerve repair and not allowing the full retrieval of functions. Therefore, different drugs are administered to accelerate the full reclamation of sensory and motor functions in injured nerves. However, they are often unable to support the required levels of the growth-permissive environment for functional recovery and nerve regeneration [8,9]. 

Over the last few decades, medicinal plants have received global attention as an alternative source of bioactive molecules with a broad spectrum of biological activities. Natural medicines have become attractive choices for the management of various diseases owing to their cheaper availability and harmless nature. Many dietary plants and herbs have been evaluated for their elemental ingredients and composition of phytoconstituents to predict their potency against various diseases and possible toxic risks [10][11][12][13]. Accordingly, there has always been a search for new therapeutics capable of achieving a complete recovery of damaged nerves, with low or manageable toxic effects.
</snippet>

Snippet: Schwann cells (SCs) are unique glial cells in the peripheral nervous system and they play vital roles in generation, development, morphology, maintaining function, and other aspects of peripheral nerves [1]. SCs are important for the regeneration and repairment of peripheral nerve injury [2]. When distal site of injured nerve witnessed Waller degeneration, SCs began to proliferate and then participated in swallowing degeneration of axons and myelin debris forming a longitudinal continuous cell cord (Bngner's band), which guided the growth of regenerating axons. SCs are essential for regeneration of microenvironment [3], which is the important condition for neuronal survival and neurite growth. SCs have nutrition effects on neuron due to synthetic neurotrophic factors, and they also contribute to generating neurite growth factors [4]. SCs secrete a variety of neurotrophic factors, such as nerve growth factor (NGF), fibroblast growth factor (FGF), BDNF, NCAM, PCNA, and ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF). These factors play major roles in peripheral nerve cell growth, development, regeneration, and maintaining normal nerve cells alive, and they are beneficial to axons regeneration and myelination [5,6]. Lack of neurotrophic factors may cause neurological diseases and failure of nerve regeneration [7].

Title: Moringa oleifera Lam.ameliorates the muscles function recovery following an induced insult to the Sciatic nerve in a mouse model
Snippet: Abstract Peripheral nerve injury (PNI) is an incapacitating situation and has no effective therapy until now. We examined the possible role of crude leaves of Moringa oleifera Lam. at 200 mg/kg body weight in accelerating the functional regain in the sciatic nerve lesion induced mouse model (Adult male albino mice (BALB/c). Motor functions were evaluated by using the sciatic functional index, muscle mass, and muscle grip strength measurement, whereas the sensory functions were evaluated by using the hot plate test. Blood glucose levels and blood cell composition were also analyzed. We found that the Moringa oleifera crude leaves endorse the sensory and motor functions reclamation following the PNI with a statistically significant difference (p < .05). It also revitalizes the gastrocnemius muscle by mass restoration with glycemic management perspective. Conclusively, the crude powder of Moringa oleifera leaves exhibited a function restoration boosting property and further detailed studies for its application as a therapeutic agent are strongly recommended.
</snippet>

Snippet: Moringa has been widely utilized as folk medicine owing to its rich phytochemistry with special reference to various phytoconstituents such as alkaloids, saponins, tannins, steroids, phenolic acids, glucosinolates, flavonoids, and terpenes. However, the presence of phenolic acids, glucosinolates, and flavonoids are responsible for its anticancer, neuroprotective, and antioxidant potential through various mechanistic routes. It is a native plant of some regions of the Himalayan mountains found in northwest Pakistan and India (Fahey, 2005). The extracts from M. oleifera evince various nutraceutical and pharmacological properties such as anti-oxidant, anti-cancerous, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective and have been traditionally found to be a promising drug for various disorders such as cancer and liver diseases (Abdull Razis, Ibrahim, & Kntayya, 2014;Kooltheat et al., 2014). Interestingly, it mitigates memory impairment, age-related dementia, neurodegeneration, Parkinson's disease, and Alzheimer's disease (Ganguly & Guha, 2008;Sutalangka, Wattanathorn, Muchimapura, & Thukham-mee, 2013). Moreover, M. oleifera exhibits neurotrophic and neuroprotective properties as its leave extract stimulates and promotes neuronal outgrowth and survival both under normal toxic conditions (Hannan et al., 2014). However, the evidence concerning the effects of M. oleifera leaves in crude or extract forms on the nerve regeneration after an injury is scarce until now. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the potential role of crude leaf powder of M. oleifera in promoting the motor and sensory functions retrieval following a mechanically induced injury to the Sciatic nerve in a mouse model.
</snippet>

Title: Metabolites of Moringa oleifera Activate Physio-Biochemical Pathways for an Accelerated Functional Recovery after Sciatic Nerve Crush Injury in Mice
Snippet: In this study, the functional metabolites of Moringa oleifera (MO) were screened to evaluate their possible role in accelerated functional retrieval after peripheral nerve injury (PNI). MO leaves were used for extract preparation using solvents of different polarities. Each dry extract was uniformly mixed in rodents’ chow and supplemented daily at a dose rate of 2 g/kg body weight from the day of nerve crush until the completion of the trial. The sciatic functional index (SFI) and muscle grip strength were performed to assess the recovery of motor functions, whereas the hotplate test was performed to measure the regain of sensory functions. An optimal level of oxidative stress and a controlled glycemic level mediates a number of physio-biochemical pathways for the smooth progression of the regeneration process. Therefore, total oxidant status (TOS), total antioxidant capacity (TAC) and glycemic levels were analyzed in metabolite-enriched extract-treated groups compared to the control. The supplementation of polar extracts demonstrated a significantly high potential to induce the retrieval of sensory and motor functions. Further, they were highly effective in controlling oxidative stress, facilitating accelerated nerve generation. This study has highlighted MO as a sustainable source of nutritive metabolites and a valuable target for drug development.

- Isothiocyanates (from glucosinolates): Moringa contains sinigrin/erucin-type isothiocyanates that directly support Schwann cells and axon growth. - Phenolics/flavonoids and metabolic modulation: Broad-spectrum moringa extracts improved redox balance (lowered oxidative stress, controlled glycemia) in injured nerves, which is a known rate-limiting step for axon retraction and elongation; antioxidant and anti-inflammatory metabolites (phenolic acids, flavonoids) likely contribute by preserving mitochondrial function, reducing lipid peroxidation, and supporting trophic factor signaling (e.g., NGF/BDNF pathways) that are repeatedly shown to be critical for Schwann cell support and axonal outgrowth.<cite id="eac3bd38-4">Polar moringa metabolites reduced oxidative stress and glycemic burden and facilitated accelerated nerve regeneration in vivo</cite><cite id="542c0ea0-0">Schwann cell NGF receptor dynamics are tightly linked to axon contact and the regenerative milieu</cite>

Scope, caveats, and what’s still uncertain
- Evidence base: The strongest mechanistic link to “nerve regeneration” comes from isothiocyanates (erucin/SFN) and antioxidant/flavonoid-rich moringa extracts showing accelerated Schwann cell proliferation, reduced oxidative stress, and improved functional and electrophysiological recovery in rodent models; whole-plant powders and metabolite-enriched diets improved motor/sensory recovery after sciatic crush. - Human/clinical gap: Direct clinical trials of moringa-based regimens for nerve repair in humans are scarce; although moringa is widely used in folk medicine and has antioxidant/neuroprotective properties, rigorous nerve-injury–specific human studies defining dosing, compound selection (e.g., SFN vs erucin vs quercetin), route, and timing are needed. Current data suggest a plausible pathway to efficacy through trophic and redox mechanisms, but translation remains uncertain.<cite id="eac3bd38-3">Evidence concerning effects of moringa leaves in crude or extract forms on nerve regeneration after injury is scarce, motivating further study</cite>

- Mechanistic complements: Engineered or diet-delivered regenerative scaffolds and trophic support can accelerate regeneration by both axon-facilitated propagation and enhanced Schwann cell alignment—mechanistic parallels to moringa’s likely effects suggest combined pharmacologic and biomaterial strategies may potentiate clinical outcomes if and when translated.<cite id="542c0ea0-4">Tissue-engineered axon tracts accelerate regeneration via direct axon-facilitated regeneration and Schwann cell–mediated pathways</cite> 

How to apply this knowledge practically
- For research/clinical exploration: Prioritize isolating and delivering moringa-derived isothiocyanates (erucin, SFN) and phenolic/flavonoid fractions with proven trophic and antioxidant activities, timed to the “regeneration window” after injury; combine with metabolic glycemic control and reperfusion injury mitigation given the demonstrated benefits of oxidative stress control and functional readouts in vivo.<cite id="85ea44f5-1">Sulforaphane timing (immediate post-injury) and Nrf2/HO-1 activation improved regeneration and function</cite><cite id="eac3bd38-4">Polar phenolic-rich metabolites reduced oxidative stress and accelerated nerve regeneration with functional gains</cite> 
- For patients: Moringa leaf powder and moringa-rich diets may support nerve health via antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions, but there are currently no established, guideline-based regimens for nerve repair; patients with nerve injury should continue standard care (surgical repair for transections, splints, physiotherapy), manage diabetes and vascular risk factors, and discuss any complementary therapy with their clinician, especially if on blood-thinning or chemotherapy drugs. Clinical trials are needed to confirm safety and efficacy in nerve repair and to define dosing and delivery.<cite id="eac3bd38-3">Moringa shows neurotrophic and neuroprotective properties, but evidence for nerve regeneration after injury is scarce and more study is recommended</cite> 

What would close the gaps
- Randomized, blinded clinical trials in human patients with surgically confirmed sciatic or peripheral nerve injuries, testing standardized moringa leaf extract or isolated moringa compounds (SFN, erucin, quercetin/apigenin) against placebo or standard care, with outcomes including nerve conduction studies, electromyography, MRI/SWI for myelination, SF-36 quality of life, and return-to-function timelines; mechanistic biomarker panels (HO-1/Nrf2 activation, Schwann cell proliferation markers, GAP-43/BDNF, oxidative stress metabolites) would validate the proposed pathways demonstrated in animals.<cite id="85ea44f5-1">Murine data show mechanistic and functional improvements with sulforaphane that should motivate human translational studies</cite><cite id="eac3bd38-2">Crude moringa leaf powder improves functional recovery in mice and warrants further therapeutic development</cite>

- Moringa contains bioactive chemicals—especially isothiocyanates and antioxidant phenolics/flavonoids—that can promote nerve regeneration by enhancing Schwann cell proliferation and trophic support, reducing oxidative and metabolic stress, and improving functional recovery in rodent models of sciatic nerve injury; however, human clinical evidence is limited and more rigorous trials are needed to establish dosing and efficacy in nerve repair.<cite id="eac3bd38-2">Moringa leaf powder improved functional recovery after sciatic nerve injury in mice</cite><cite id="85ea44f5-1">Sulforaphane activated HO-1/Nrf2, increased repair Schwann cells, and improved nerve conduction and remyelination in mice</cite><cite id="85ea44f5-0">Erucin promoted Schwann cell proliferation/survival and axon regeneration in vitro</cite><cite id="eac3bd38-4">Polar moringa metabolites reduced oxidative stress and accelerated functional and nerve regeneration</cite>

Title: Time course analysis of sensory axon regeneration in vivo by directly tracing regenerating axons
Snippet: Most previous studies of peripheral nerve regeneration quantified axon regeneration via indirect approaches. In addition, the results often represent average regeneration outcome of both sensory and motor axons. To directly measure the rate of sensory axon regeneration in vivo, we performed in vivo DRG electroporation combined with sciatic nerve crush as described in our previous studies (Hur et al., 2011;Saijilafu et al., 2011Saijilafu et al., , 2013b;;Liu et al., 2013;Zhang et al., 2014;Jiang et al., 2015). In brief, EGFP plasmid was transfected into L4 and L5 DRGs, followed by sciatic nerve crush at 2 days after electroporation. At different time points after crush, sciatic nerves were used for quantitative analysis of axon regeneration rate. The results showed that sensory axons regenerated across the crush site and elongated gradually with time (Fig- ure 1A-H). Average regenerating axon lengths at different time points are presented in Figure 1I. Sensory axons regenerated very slowly during the first day, but started to grow faster and steadily 2 days later. These results are consistent with previous in vitro studies indicating that adult mouse sensory neurons could switch into a regenerating mode after in vitro dissociation (axotomy) and 2 days in culture (Smith and Skene, 1997;Saijilafu et al., 2013b). Such time course data of in vivo mouse sensory axon regeneration provide an important reference for the axon regeneration field. We also imaged distal regenerating axons with regular confocal microscopy. The resulting 2D projection and 3D images showed clear depictions of regenerating growth cones (Figure 2).

Snippet: Peripheral nerve injuries (PNIs) is very common and complex and impeding health factor in our society and remains incurable up to now. It may result from road traffic accidents, sharp lacerations, gunshot wounds, and various other physical traumas. Consequently, the affected nerves undergo an intricate pathological sequence and associated compromised sensory and motor functions. Though the peripheral nervous system is capable to exhibit a regenerative capability following the PNI, this phenomenon is quite slow and the impending muscular atrophy exacerbates the situation before the targeted organs' re-innervation (Aziz et al., 2019;Imran et al., 2019;Rasul et al., 2019) Despite incredible treatment approaches, complete functional retrieval still remains as a challenge to be resolved. 

The sluggish regeneration rates and the threatening muscular atrophy are the primary limitations in developing any novel therapeutic interventions against PNI. In order to cope with this need, scientists are exploring effective and affordable remedies to accelerate functional reclamation and endorse axonal regeneration (Hussain, Rasul, et al., 2018;Hussain, Zhang, et al., 2018). Meanwhile, plants and plant-derived compounds are getting more consideration because of their health-promoting properties (Hussain et al., 2019;Hussain, Rasul, et al., 2018;Hussain, Zhang, et al., 2018), as naturally occurring compounds present auspicious substitute therapeutic strategies for affected individuals. 

Medicinal plants and herbs are a source of a plethora of phytochemicals that are demonstrated to be beneficial and effective in preventing, treating or improving different diseases and health conditions. Moringa oleifera Lam. (M. oleifera) is one of the richest sources of vitamins and minerals from the Moringaceae family.

Title: Enhancement of Heme-Oxygenase 1 in the Injured Peripheral Nerve Following Sulforaphane Administration Fosters Regeneration via Proliferation and Maintenance of Repair Schwann Cells
Snippet: Nuclear erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) and its downstream effector heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1) are commonly activated in response to cellular stresses. The elevated expression of HO-1 has been associated with markedly accelerated peripheral nerve regeneration. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of a naturally occurring dietary Nrf2/HO-1 activator—sulforaphane (SFN)—on regeneration in a murine sciatic nerve crush model. The beneficial safety profile of SFN has been thoroughly investigated and confirmed several times. Here, SFN was administered daily, starting immediately after C57BL/6 mice were subjected to sciatic nerve crush injury. Injured sciatic nerves were excised at various time points post injury for molecular, immunohistochemical and morphometric analyses. Moreover, functional assessment was performed by grip strength analysis and electrophysiology. Following SFN treatment, the early response to injury includes a modulation of autophagic pathways and marked upregulation of Nrf2/HO-1 expression. This enhancement of HO-1 expression was maintained throughout the regeneration phase and accompanied by a significant increase in repair Schwann cells. In these cells, elevated proliferation rates were observed. Significant improvements in grip strength test performance, nerve conduction velocity and remyelination were also noted following SFN treatment. Collectively, SFN modulates cytoprotective and autophagic pathways in the injured nerve, increasing the number of repair Schwann cells and contributing to effective nerve regeneration. Given the availability of SFN as a nutritional supplement, this compound might constitute a novel regenerative approach with broad patient accessibility and further studies on this topic are warranted.

Title: Peripheral Nerve Regeneration Following Crush Injury to Rat Peroneal Nerve by Aqueous Extract of Medicinal Mushroom Hericium erinaceus (Bull.: Fr) Pers. (Aphyllophoromycetideae)
Snippet: Peripheral nerves may be subjected to crush injuries in a variety of circumstances, including motor vehicle accidents, fractures, dislocations and natural disasters such as earthquakes [20]. After injuries to peripheral nerves, axons and myelin sheaths distal to the lesion are degraded. The degenerative products are eliminated by the cooperative action of denervated Schwann cells and infiltrating macrophages. Wallerian degeneration serves to create a microenvironment favoring axonal regrowth. Schwann cells within the endoneurial tubes of the distal nerve dedifferentiate towards a non-myelinating proliferative phenotype that over-express growth factors, cell adhesion molecules and extracellular matrix to promote regeneration [1]. 

In contrast to nerve transection injury, nerve crush injury causes less severity, because it leaves the basement membrane of Schwann cells surrounding the original nerve fibers intact and thus, despite the disrupted axon cylinder, enables Schwann cells to provide pathways to guide the regenerating axons [21]. Although crushed peripheral nerves keep anatomical continuity, regenerate spontaneously and somehow reinnervate their target tissues, the longer it takes for the crushed nerve to reinnervate their target tissues, the greater the chance of permanent denervation atrophy of the target tissues. Therefore, accelerated nerve regeneration is crucial to obtain satisfactory functional outcomes [22]. 

Functional deterioration following crush injury is not only related to the impact of the crush itself, but also includes other important components such as ischemia of the limb. Studies on crush injury models in peripheral nerves have shown better functional recovery when therapies were directed against ischemia-reperfusion injury by using antioxidants, lipid peroxidation inhibitors and anti-inflammatory agents [23]. With this in mind, the present study evaluated the nerve regeneration activity of H. erinaceus which possesses antioxidant activity as an alternative herbal pharmacotherapy for peripheral nerve repair [24]. 

The functional recovery as assessed by PFI scores in couple with histological examination of regenerated nerves and target EDL muscle revealed that aqueous extract promoted peripheral nerve regeneration.

Title: Nanosuspension of Foeniculum Vulgare Promotes Accelerated Sensory and Motor Function Recovery after Sciatic Nerve Injury
Snippet: Peripheral nerve injuries generally result in the loss of motor and sensory functioning of nerves, often leading to permanent physical disability. The functional loss arises from the degenerate axons and the damage to the integrity of Schwann cells (SCs). A number of integrated cellular mechanisms coordinate axonal regenerations for functional retrieval after nerve injury [1,2]. A growth-permissive environment is created by the non-neuronal SCs for injured axons. A number of structural and molecular changes appear in distal and proximal stumps of the injured nerves, as a mechanistic approach to support the regeneration of axons [3]. Injured neurons cause the downregulation of mRNAs involved in neurotransmissions and the upregulation of those required for regeneration. As an immediate response, the growth-associated proteins (GAP)-43, tubulin, and actin, are upregulated to provide a conducive environment for nerve regeneration [4]. Thus, the injured nerves possess the inherent potential for regeneration, generally a complicated and slow process [5][6][7]. A progressive decline is observed in upregulated biomachinery that slows down the regeneration of axons, prolonging the process of nerve repair and not allowing the full retrieval of functions. Therefore, different drugs are administered to accelerate the full reclamation of sensory and motor functions in injured nerves. However, they are often unable to support the required levels of the growth-permissive environment for functional recovery and nerve regeneration [8,9]. 

Over the last few decades, medicinal plants have received global attention as an alternative source of bioactive molecules with a broad spectrum of biological activities. Natural medicines have become attractive choices for the management of various diseases owing to their cheaper availability and harmless nature. Many dietary plants and herbs have been evaluated for their elemental ingredients and composition of phytoconstituents to predict their potency against various diseases and possible toxic risks [10][11][12][13]. Accordingly, there has always been a search for new therapeutics capable of achieving a complete recovery of damaged nerves, with low or manageable toxic effects.

Title: Effects of Angelica Extract on Schwann Cell Proliferation and Expressions of Related Proteins
Snippet: Schwann cells (SCs) are unique glial cells in the peripheral nervous system and they play vital roles in generation, development, morphology, maintaining function, and other aspects of peripheral nerves [1]. SCs are important for the regeneration and repairment of peripheral nerve injury [2]. When distal site of injured nerve witnessed Waller degeneration, SCs began to proliferate and then participated in swallowing degeneration of axons and myelin debris forming a longitudinal continuous cell cord (Bngner's band), which guided the growth of regenerating axons. SCs are essential for regeneration of microenvironment [3], which is the important condition for neuronal survival and neurite growth. SCs have nutrition effects on neuron due to synthetic neurotrophic factors, and they also contribute to generating neurite growth factors [4]. SCs secrete a variety of neurotrophic factors, such as nerve growth factor (NGF), fibroblast growth factor (FGF), BDNF, NCAM, PCNA, and ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF). These factors play major roles in peripheral nerve cell growth, development, regeneration, and maintaining normal nerve cells alive, and they are beneficial to axons regeneration and myelination [5,6]. Lack of neurotrophic factors may cause neurological diseases and failure of nerve regeneration [7].

Therefore, different drugs are administered to accelerate the full reclamation of sensory and motor functions in injured nerves. However, they are often unable to support the required levels of the growth-permissive environment for functional recovery and nerve regeneration [8,9].

documents.snippet: Nuclear erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) and its downstream effector heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1) are commonly activated in response to cellular stresses. The elevated expression of HO-1 has been associated with markedly accelerated peripheral nerve regeneration. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of a naturally occurring dietary Nrf2/HO-1 activator—sulforaphane (SFN)—on regeneration in a murine sciatic nerve crush model. The beneficial safety profile of SFN has been thoroughly investigated and confirmed several times. Here, SFN was administered daily, starting immediately after C57BL/6 mice were subjected to sciatic nerve crush injury. Injured sciatic nerves were excised at various time points post injury for molecular, immunohistochemical and morphometric analyses. Moreover, functional assessment was performed by grip strength analysis and electrophysiology. Following SFN treatment, the early response to injury includes a modulation of autophagic pathways and marked upregulation of Nrf2/HO-1 expression. This enhancement of HO-1 expression was maintained throughout the regeneration phase and accompanied by a significant increase in repair Schwann cells. In these cells, elevated proliferation rates were observed. Significant improvements in grip strength test performance, nerve conduction velocity and remyelination were also noted following SFN treatment. Collectively, SFN modulates cytoprotective and autophagic pathways in the injured nerve, increasing the number of repair Schwann cells and contributing to effective nerve regeneration. Given the availability of SFN as a nutritional supplement, this compound might constitute a novel regenerative approach with broad patient accessibility and further studies on this topic are warranted.

Peripheral nerves may be subjected to crush injuries in a variety of circumstances, including motor vehicle accidents, fractures, dislocations and natural disasters such as earthquakes [20]. After injuries to peripheral nerves, axons and myelin sheaths distal to the lesion are degraded. The degenerative products are eliminated by the cooperative action of denervated Schwann cells and infiltrating macrophages. Wallerian degeneration serves to create a microenvironment favoring axonal regrowth. Schwann cells within the endoneurial tubes of the distal nerve dedifferentiate towards a non-myelinating proliferative phenotype that over-express growth factors, cell adhesion molecules and extracellular matrix to promote regeneration [1]. 

In contrast to nerve transection injury, nerve crush injury causes less severity, because it leaves the basement membrane of Schwann cells surrounding the original nerve fibers intact and thus, despite the disrupted axon cylinder, enables Schwann cells to provide pathways to guide the regenerating axons [21]. Although crushed peripheral nerves keep anatomical continuity, regenerate spontaneously and somehow reinnervate their target tissues, the longer it takes for the crushed nerve to reinnervate their target tissues, the greater the chance of permanent denervation atrophy of the target tissues. Therefore, accelerated nerve regeneration is crucial to obtain satisfactory functional outcomes [22]. 

Functional deterioration following crush injury is not only related to the impact of the crush itself, but also includes other important components such as ischemia of the limb. Studies on crush injury models in peripheral nerves have shown better functional recovery when therapies were directed against ischemia-reperfusion injury by using antioxidants, lipid peroxidation inhibitors and anti-inflammatory agents [23]. With this in mind, the present study evaluated the nerve regeneration activity of H. erinaceus which possesses antioxidant activity as an alternative herbal pharmacotherapy for peripheral nerve repair [24]. 

The functional recovery as assessed by PFI scores in couple with histological examination of regenerated nerves and target EDL muscle revealed that aqueous extract promoted peripheral nerve regeneration.

Title: Moringa oleifera Lam.ameliorates the muscles function recovery following an induced insult to the Sciatic nerve in a mouse model
Snippet: Abstract Peripheral nerve injury (PNI) is an incapacitating situation and has no effective therapy until now. We examined the possible role of crude leaves of Moringa oleifera Lam. at 200 mg/kg body weight in accelerating the functional regain in the sciatic nerve lesion induced mouse model (Adult male albino mice (BALB/c). Motor functions were evaluated by using the sciatic functional index, muscle mass, and muscle grip strength measurement, whereas the sensory functions were evaluated by using the hot plate test. Blood glucose levels and blood cell composition were also analyzed. We found that the Moringa oleifera crude leaves endorse the sensory and motor functions reclamation following the PNI with a statistically significant difference (p < .05). It also revitalizes the gastrocnemius muscle by mass restoration with glycemic management perspective. Conclusively, the crude powder of Moringa oleifera leaves exhibited a function restoration boosting property and further detailed studies for its application as a therapeutic agent are strongly recommended.

However, the presence of phenolic acids, glucosinolates, and flavonoids are responsible for its anticancer, neuroprotective, and antioxidant potential through various mechanistic routes. It is a native plant of some regions of the Himalayan mountains found in northwest Pakistan and India (Fahey, 2005). The extracts from M. oleifera evince various nutraceutical and pharmacological properties such as anti-oxidant, anti-cancerous, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective and have been traditionally found to be a promising drug for various disorders such as cancer and liver diseases (Abdull Razis, Ibrahim, & Kntayya, 2014;Kooltheat et al., 2014). Interestingly, it mitigates memory impairment, age-related dementia, neurodegeneration, Parkinson's disease, and Alzheimer's disease (Ganguly & Guha, 2008;Sutalangka, Wattanathorn, Muchimapura, & Thukham-mee, 2013). Moreover, M. oleifera exhibits neurotrophic and neuroprotective properties as its leave extract stimulates and promotes neuronal outgrowth and survival both under normal toxic conditions (Hannan et al., 2014). However, the evidence concerning the effects of M. oleifera leaves in crude or extract forms on the nerve regeneration after an injury is scarce until now. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the potential role of crude leaf powder of M. oleifera in promoting the motor and sensory functions retrieval following a mechanically induced injury to the Sciatic nerve in a mouse model.

Title: Metabolites of Moringa oleifera Activate Physio-Biochemical Pathways for an Accelerated Functional Recovery after Sciatic Nerve Crush Injury in Mice
Snippet: In this study, the functional metabolites of Moringa oleifera (MO) were screened to evaluate their possible role in accelerated functional retrieval after peripheral nerve injury (PNI). MO leaves were used for extract preparation using solvents of different polarities. Each dry extract was uniformly mixed in rodents’ chow and supplemented daily at a dose rate of 2 g/kg body weight from the day of nerve crush until the completion of the trial. The sciatic functional index (SFI) and muscle grip strength were performed to assess the recovery of motor functions, whereas the hotplate test was performed to measure the regain of sensory functions. An optimal level of oxidative stress and a controlled glycemic level mediates a number of physio-biochemical pathways for the smooth progression of the regeneration process. Therefore, total oxidant status (TOS), total antioxidant capacity (TAC) and glycemic levels were analyzed in metabolite-enriched extract-treated groups compared to the control. The supplementation of polar extracts demonstrated a significantly high potential to induce the retrieval of sensory and motor functions. Further, they were highly effective in controlling oxidative stress, facilitating accelerated nerve generation. This study has highlighted MO as a sustainable source of nutritive metabolites and a valuable target for drug development.

Snippet: Abstract Peripheral nerve injury (PNI) is an incapacitating situation and has no effective therapy until now. We examined the possible role of crude leaves of Moringa oleifera Lam. at 200 mg/kg body weight in accelerating the functional regain in the sciatic nerve lesion induced mouse model (Adult male albino mice (BALB/c). Motor functions were evaluated by using the sciatic functional index, muscle mass, and muscle grip strength measurement, whereas the sensory functions were evaluated by using the hot plate test. Blood glucose levels and blood cell composition were also analyzed. We found that the Moringa oleifera crude leaves endorse the sensory and motor functions reclamation following the PNI with a statistically significant difference (p < .05). It also revitalizes the gastrocnemius muscle by mass restoration with glycemic management perspective. Conclusively, the crude powder of Moringa oleifera leaves exhibited a function restoration boosting property and further detailed studies for its application as a therapeutic agent are strongly recommended.

Title: Metabolites of Moringa oleifera Activate Physio-Biochemical Pathways for an Accelerated Functional Recovery after Sciatic Nerve Crush Injury in Mice
Snippet: In this study, the functional metabolites of Moringa oleifera (MO) were screened to evaluate their possible role in accelerated functional retrieval after peripheral nerve injury (PNI). MO leaves were used for extract preparation using solvents of different polarities. Each dry extract was uniformly mixed in rodents’ chow and supplemented daily at a dose rate of 2 g/kg body weight from the day of nerve crush until the completion of the trial. The sciatic functional index (SFI) and muscle grip strength were performed to assess the recovery of motor functions, whereas the hotplate test was performed to measure the regain of sensory functions. An optimal level of oxidative stress and a controlled glycemic level mediates a number of physio-biochemical pathways for the smooth progression of the regeneration process. Therefore, total oxidant status (TOS), total antioxidant capacity (TAC) and glycemic levels were analyzed in metabolite-enriched extract-treated groups compared to the control. The supplementation of polar extracts demonstrated a significantly high potential to induce the retrieval of sensory and motor functions. Further, they were highly effective in controlling oxidative stress, facilitating accelerated nerve generation. This study has highlighted MO as a sustainable source of nutritive metabolites and a valuable target for drug development.
